headline: Hannō was coined by Iwakawa Tomotarō in 1884 as a translation of English reaction, and the ō of 応 became nō by renjō.

sources.quote: Coined by Japanese educator and zoologist Iwakawa Tomotarō in 1884 in his work 生物学語彙 (Seibutsugaku goi, “A biological vocabulary in English, Latin and Japanese”) as a translation of English reaction.
The ō reading for 応 changes to nō as an instance of renjō (連(れん)声(じょう)).

meaning: to add one thing to another
headline: Tsukekuwaeru is 付け (tsuke, the stem of 付ける (tsukeru, “to attach”)) plus 加える (kuwaeru, “to add”).

sources.quote: From 付(つ)け (tsuke, 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 付(つ)ける (tsukeru, “to attach”)) + 加(くわ)える (kuwaeru, “to add”)

headline: Mine is 御 (mi, honorific prefix) plus 峰 (ne, “peak”), in reference to the 神 (kami, “god or spirit”) at the top of a mountain.

sources.quote: From 御(み) (mi, honorific prefix) + 峰(ね) (ne, “peak”), in reference to the 神 (kami, “god or spirit”) at the top of a mountain. Now the standard spelling for a peak.
Compare 道 (michi, “road”).

meaning: good or bad, merits or demerits, quality
headline: Yoshiashi is 善し (“classical Japanese of now 良い (yoi)”) plus 悪し (“classical Japanese synonym of 悪い (warui)”).

sources.quote: From 善し (“classical Japanese of now 良(よ)い (yoi)”) + 悪し (“classical Japanese synonym of 悪(わる)い (warui)”).

headline: Hōkai is from Middle Chinese 崩潰, and 壊 (kai) is a daiyōji replacing 潰 (kai).

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 崩潰 (MC pong hwojH). 壊 (kai) is a daiyōji replacing 潰 (kai).

headline: Nadare is the stem of the classical verb 傾る (nadaru), and its kanji spelling is jukujikun, borrowed from Chinese 雪崩 (xuěbēng).

sources.quote: The 連用形 (ren'yōkei, stem or continuative form) of the classical verb 傾る (nadaru), modern 雪崩れる, 傾れる (nadareru, “to slope, descend; of snow, to slide”).
The kanji spelling is jukujikun (熟(じゅく)字(じ)訓(くん)), borrowed from Chinese 雪崩 (xuěbēng).

headline: Koyomi is generally considered a shift from 日 (ka, “day”) plus 読み (yomi, “reading; counting”), literally “day counting”.

sources.quote: Dictionaries generally consider this equivalent to or a shift from a compound of 日(か) (ka, “day”) + 読(よ)み (yomi, “reading; counting”, the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 読(よ)む (yomu, “to read; to count”)). Literally, “day counting”.

headline: Kokoroyoi is 心 (kokoro, “heart”) plus 良い (yoi, “good”).

sources.quote: From 心 (kokoro, “heart”) + 良い (yoi, “good”).

headline: Yūrei is from the Middle Chinese compound 幽靈, literally “dark + supernatural”.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese compound 幽靈 /幽灵 (ʔjiw leng, literally “dark + supernatural”). Compare modern Mandarin reading yōulíng, Min Nan iu-lêng.

meaning: to plan, to intend, to aspire to
headline: Kokorozasu is 心 (kokoro, “heart; mind”) plus 指す (sasu, “to point”), first cited to the mid-900s.

sources.quote: Compound of 心 (kokoro, “heart; mind”) + 指す (sasu, “to point”), literally in reference to where one's thoughts are focused on.
First cited to the mid-900s.

headline: Yayakoshii is an adjectivization of 稚児 (yayako, “infant”), from the way infants are fretful and complicated to deal with.

sources.quote: Adjectivization of 稚児(ややこ) (yayako, “infant”), from the way infants are fretful and complicated to deal with.

headline: Kokorozashi is the continuative stem of the verb 志す (kokorozasu, “to intend to do something, to aspire to do something”).

sources.quote: The 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “continuative or stem form”) of verb 志す (kokorozasu, “to intend to do something, to aspire to do something”).

headline: Imada is from Old Japanese, first appearing in the Kojiki of 712 CE, and ultimately from Proto-Japonic.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese, first appearing in the Kojiki of 712 CE; ultimately from Proto-Japonic *imanta. Cognate with Okinawan なーだ (nāda, “yet”).
